paragraphs.heading: The first of the big five
paragraphs.text: The Late Ordovician mass extinction, also called the end-Ordovician or Ordovician–Silurian extinction, struck roughly 445 million years ago. It is the first of the "big five" mass extinctions in Earth's history. It reached across the whole globe, wiping out 49–60% of marine genera and close to 85% of marine species. At the time, most complex many-celled life lived in the sea, and the only trace of life on land is rare spores from small early plants.

paragraphs.heading: How big it was
paragraphs.text: Measured by the share of genera lost, it is often ranked the second largest known extinction, behind only the end-Permian event. Counting genera is seen as more reliable than counting species, and by that count about 100 marine families disappeared. Every major group of the time was hit. A third of all brachiopod and bryozoan families vanished, along with many groups of conodonts, trilobites, echinoderms, corals, bivalves and graptolites.

paragraphs.heading: The first pulse brought ice
paragraphs.text: The extinction is usually described as two separate pulses. The first, called LOMEI-1, began where the Katian stage of the Late Ordovician gives way to the Hirnantian stage. It is usually blamed on a glaciation that spread quickly over Gondwana, switching Earth from a greenhouse climate to an icehouse one. Cooling and falling sea levels took away habitat on the continental shelves, hitting hardest those creatures with narrow home ranges and a low tolerance for changes in temperature. During the cold spell, sea life partly bounced back, and a new cold-water community called the Hirnantia fauna took hold.

paragraphs.heading: The second pulse brought warmth
paragraphs.text: The second pulse, LOMEI-2, came in the later Hirnantian, when the ice pulled back quickly and warm conditions returned. It came with anoxia, meaning a loss of oxygen, and euxinia, the build-up of toxic sulfide, on a worldwide scale. These conditions lasted into the following Rhuddanian stage of the Silurian period. The Hirnantia fauna died out in this pulse and was replaced by Silurian communities suited to warmer water. Some researchers argue for a third pulse in the early Rhuddanian, while others see it as the tail of a longer second pulse.

paragraphs.heading: Winners and losers
paragraphs.text: The groups did not all fare alike. The first pulse fell hardest on deep-water species and on tropical species found only in particular seas. The Foliomena fauna, a set of thin-shelled animals suited to deep water with little oxygen, vanished completely; since it had been widespread and hardy before, its sudden end suggests its special habitat disappeared. Among brachiopods, the older inarticulate kinds never regained their earlier diversity, while groups such as the Spiriferida and Atrypida were hit less and spread out afterwards. Brachiopods that were more abundant were also more likely to survive.

paragraphs.heading: A quick recovery
paragraphs.text: Diversity climbed back to its earlier level over the first 5 million years of the Silurian. Early Silurian communities were at first simpler, with species living broader ways of life. Faunas that had been highly local in the Late Ordovician gave way to some of the most widespread faunas of the whole Phanerozoic, a pattern that held through most of the Silurian. Compared with the Permian–Triassic and Cretaceous–Paleogene extinctions, this one left few long-term marks on ecosystems, and life recovered much faster than after the Permian–Triassic event.
